reference.source: Standard breast surgery textbook and benign breast disease guidance
clinicalPearls: Mondor disease is superficial thrombophlebitis of the subcutaneous veins of the breast and anterior chest wall, most often the thoracoepigastric or lateral thoracic vein
It typically presents as a sudden, tender, cord-like subcutaneous structure that becomes more visible when the skin is stretched or the arm is raised
A characteristic skin dimple or groove may form along the line of the thrombosed vein, which can raise concern for underlying malignancy
The condition is usually self-limiting and benign, and recognising the palpable cord is key to avoiding unnecessary alarm
Recognised precipitants include local trauma, breast surgery, tight garments, strenuous exertion, and dehydration, although many cases are idiopathic
Because the tethering and dimpling can mimic carcinoma, imaging as part of triple assessment is used to reassure and exclude an underlying cancer
Management is conservative with reassurance, warmth, and simple analgesia, and the cord typically resolves over several weeks
An associated breast lump or atypical features should prompt full assessment, as Mondor disease can occasionally accompany an underlying malignancy
reference.pathophysiology: Mondor disease is a localised thrombophlebitis affecting the superficial veins that drain the breast and adjacent chest wall. Thrombosis of the vein, together with an inflammatory reaction in and around the vessel wall, converts the vein into a firm, tender, palpable cord. As the process organises and the vein retracts, traction on the overlying skin produces the characteristic linear groove or dimple. The trigger is often venous stasis or endothelial injury from trauma, surgery, or compression, in keeping with the classic contributors to thrombosis, though a proportion of cases have no identifiable cause.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination demonstrating a tender palpable cord and skin groove
Ultrasound to confirm a thrombosed superficial vein and exclude an underlying mass
Mammography in women of appropriate age as part of triple assessment
Core biopsy of any associated discrete lump
Assessment for precipitating factors such as recent trauma or surgery
redFlags: An associated discrete breast lump or suspicious imaging finding
Skin changes beyond a simple linear groove, such as thickening or peau d'orange
Failure of the cord to resolve within the expected timeframe
Recurrent or migratory thrombophlebitis suggesting an underlying systemic or thrombophilic cause
reference.prognosis: Mondor disease is benign and self-limiting, with the thrombosed cord typically resolving spontaneously over a few weeks with conservative measures, and recurrence is uncommon.
pitfalls: Mistaking the skin dimpling for a sign of carcinoma and alarming the patient without imaging
Failing to exclude an underlying malignancy, which can rarely coexist
Over-treating a self-limiting condition with anticoagulation or surgery
Overlooking an underlying thrombophilia in recurrent or migratory cases
Not addressing modifiable precipitants such as tight garments
references: Standard breast surgery reference text on benign breast disease
Guidance on evaluation of breast skin changes
management: Conservative supportive care as the condition is benign and self-limiting, with reassurance, simple analgesia or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and warm compresses
Identify and address precipitants such as local trauma, tight garments, strenuous exertion and dehydration
Complete triple assessment with clinical examination, ultrasound and age-appropriate mammography to exclude an underlying breast carcinoma, since tethering and dimpling can mimic malignancy
Advise temporary restriction of strenuous upper-limb activity during the acute phase to aid resolution of the thrombosed cord
Monitor for spontaneous resolution and consider evaluation for an underlying thrombophilia or malignancy if the condition is recurrent or atypical
